title: No. 6 — Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The three previous papers have been devoted to enumerating the dangers we would face, in a state of disunion, from the arms and arts of foreign nations. I will now turn to dangers of a different and perhaps still more alarming kind—those that will in all probability flow from disputes between the States themselves, and from domestic factions and upheavals. These have already been touched on in some places; but they deserve fuller and more particular investigation.

A man must be far gone in utopian speculations who can seriously doubt that, if these States were either wholly disunited or only united in partial confederacies, the subdivisions into which they might be thrown would have frequent and violent conflicts with one another. To assume there are no motives for such conflicts, and to use that as an argument against their occurrence, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious. To expect continued harmony among a number of independent, unconnected sovereignties in the same neighborhood would be to ignore the uniform course of human events and defy the accumulated experience of the ages.

The causes of hostility among nations are countless. Some operate broadly and almost constantly on the collective bodies of society. Of this kind are the love of power, or the desire of pre-eminence and dominion; and the jealousy of power, or the desire of equality and safety. Others have a more limited but equally active influence within their spheres. Such are the rivalries and competitions of commerce among commercial nations. And still others, no less numerous than the former, originate entirely in private passions—in the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals in the communities they belong to. Men of this class, whether favorites of a king or of a people, have in too many instances abused the confidence placed in them, and, claiming some public motive as a pretext, have not hesitated to sacrifice national tranquility to personal advantage or personal gratification.

The famous Pericles, in deference to the resentment of a prostitute,(1) attacked, defeated, and destroyed the city of the SAMIANS at the cost of much blood and treasure of his countrymen. The same man, driven by private spite against the MEGARIANS,(2) another nation of Greece—or to escape a prosecution with which he was threatened as accomplice in a supposed theft by the sculptor Phidias,(3) or to dodge accusations being prepared against him for squandering state funds in the purchase of popularity,(4) or by some combination of all these causes—was the original author of that famous and fatal war known in Grecian annals as the PELOPONNESIAN war, which, after various reverses, pauses, and renewals, ended in the ruin of the Athenian commonwealth.

The ambitious cardinal who was prime minister to Henry VIII, allowing his vanity to aspire to the triple crown,(5) hoped to win that splendid prize through the influence of the Emperor Charles V. To secure the favor and interest of this enterprising and powerful monarch, he plunged England into a war with France, contrary to the plainest dictates of policy and at the risk of the safety and independence not only of the kingdom he ruled by his counsels but of Europe in general. For if there ever was a sovereign who came near to realizing the project of universal monarchy, it was the Emperor Charles V, of whose intrigues Wolsey was at once the instrument and the dupe.

The influence which the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the contemporary policy, ferments, and pacifications of a considerable part of Europe are subjects too often discussed not to be generally known.

To multiply examples of the agency of personal considerations in producing great national events—whether foreign or domestic, depending on their direction—would be a needless waste of time. Those who have even a superficial acquaintance with the sources from which they may be drawn will themselves recall a variety of instances; and those who have a tolerable knowledge of human nature will not need such evidence to form their opinion either of the reality or the extent of that agency. Still, a reference illustrating the general principle may fittingly be made to a case that has lately occurred among ourselves. If Shays had not been a DESPERATE DEBTOR, it is much to be doubted whether Massachusetts would have been plunged into a civil war.

But notwithstanding the concurring testimony of experience on this point, there are still to be found visionary or designing men ready to advocate the paradox of perpetual peace among the States, even though dismembered and alienated from each other. The genius of republics (they say) is peaceful; the spirit of commerce tends to soften men's manners and to extinguish those inflammable humors that have so often kindled into wars. Commercial republics, like ours, will never be inclined to waste themselves in ruinous quarrels with each other. They will be governed by mutual interest and will cultivate a spirit of mutual amity and concord.

Is it not (we may ask these political projectors) the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit? If this is their true interest, have they in fact pursued it? Has it not, on the contrary, invariably been found that momentary passions and immediate interest exercise a more active and imperious control over human conduct than general or remote considerations of policy, utility, or justice? Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies? Are the former not administered by MEN as well as the latter? Are there not aversions, preferences, rivalries, and desires for unjust acquisitions that affect nations as well as kings? Are popular assemblies not frequently subject to impulses of rage, resentment, jealousy, greed, and other irregular and violent propensities? Is it not well known that their decisions are often governed by a few individuals in whom they place confidence, and are therefore liable to be tinged by the passions and views of those individuals? Has commerce so far done anything more than change the objects of war? Is the love of wealth not as domineering and enterprising a passion as that of power or glory? Have there not been as many wars founded upon commercial motives, since commerce became the prevailing system of nations, as were before caused by the lust for territory or dominion? Has the spirit of commerce not, in many instances, supplied new incentives to both these appetites? Let experience, the least fallible guide of human opinion, be appealed to for an answer to these questions.

Sparta, Athens, Rome, and Carthage were all republics; two of them, Athens and Carthage, were of the commercial kind. Yet they were as often engaged in wars, offensive and defensive, as the neighboring monarchies of the same times. Sparta was little more than a well-regulated camp; and Rome was never sated of carnage and conquest.

Carthage, though a commercial republic, was the aggressor in the very war that ended in her destruction. Hannibal had carried her arms into the heart of Italy and to the gates of Rome before Scipio, in turn, defeated him in the territories of Carthage and made a conquest of the commonwealth.

Venice, in later times, figured more than once in wars of ambition, until, becoming a target for the other Italian states, Pope Julius II found means to forge that formidable league(9) which dealt a deadly blow to the power and pride of this haughty republic.

The provinces of Holland, until they were overwhelmed by debt and taxes, took a leading and conspicuous part in the wars of Europe. They had furious contests with England for dominion of the sea, and were among the most persistent and implacable opponents of Louis XIV.

In the government of Britain, the representatives of the people make up one branch of the national legislature. Commerce has for ages been the predominant pursuit of that country. Yet few nations have been more frequently engaged in war, and many of the wars in which that kingdom has been engaged have proceeded from the people.

There have been, if I may put it this way, almost as many popular as royal wars. The cries of the nation and the demands of their representatives have, on various occasions, dragged their monarchs into war or kept them in it, contrary to their inclinations and sometimes contrary to the real interests of the State. In that memorable struggle for supremacy between the rival houses of AUSTRIA and BOURBON, which so long kept Europe in flames, it is well known that the antipathies of the English against the French, supporting the ambition—or rather the avarice—of a favorite leader,(10) prolonged the war beyond the limits set by sound policy, and for a considerable time in opposition to the views of the court.

The wars of these two last-mentioned nations have largely grown out of commercial concerns: the desire to supplant and the fear of being supplanted, either in particular branches of trade or in the general advantages of trade and navigation, and sometimes even the more culpable desire of sharing in the commerce of other nations without their consent.

The most recent war between Britain and Spain sprang from the British merchants' attempts to carry on illicit trade with the Spanish main. These unjustifiable practices on their side produced harshness on the Spanish side toward British subjects—harshness no more justifiable, since it exceeded the bounds of just retaliation and was chargeable with inhumanity and cruelty. Many of the English who were captured on the Spanish coast were sent to dig in the mines of Potosi; and by the usual progress of a spirit of resentment, the innocent were after a while lumped in with the guilty in indiscriminate punishment. The complaints of the merchants kindled a violent flame throughout the nation, which soon broke out in the House of Commons and was passed from there to the ministry. Letters of reprisal were issued, and a war ensued that, in its consequences, overthrew all the alliances which only twenty years before had been formed with sanguine expectations of the most beneficial fruits.

From this summary of what has happened in other countries whose situations have most closely resembled our own, what reason can we have to trust those reveries that would seduce us into expecting peace and cordiality between the members of the present confederacy in a state of separation? Have we not already seen enough of the falsity and extravagance of those idle theories that have amused us with promises of exemption from the imperfections, weaknesses, and evils inherent in society in every form? Is it not time to wake from the deceitful dream of a golden age and to adopt as a practical maxim, for the direction of our political conduct, that we, like the other inhabitants of the globe, are still far from the happy realm of perfect wisdom and perfect virtue?

Let the extreme low point to which our national dignity and credit have sunk, the inconveniences felt everywhere from a lax and ill administration of government, the revolt of part of the State of North Carolina, the recent menacing disturbances in Pennsylvania, and the actual insurrections and rebellions in Massachusetts—let all these declare!

So far is the general sense of mankind from agreeing with the doctrines of those who try to lull our fears of discord and hostility between the States, in the event of disunion, that long observation of the progress of society has made it a sort of political axiom that proximity, or nearness of situation, makes nations natural enemies. An intelligent writer expresses himself on this subject to the following effect: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions, extinguishing that secret jealousy which disposes all states to aggrandize themselves at the expense of their neighbors."(11) This passage at once points out the EVIL and suggests the REMEDY.
